topics.label: AI Literacy & Capability
topics.description: Critical capabilities needed to become AI fluent — frameworks, competencies, and workforce readiness.

articles.title: Developing a competency framework for artificial intelligence in undergraduate dental education - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Developing a competency framework for artificial intelligence in undergraduate dental education  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited to dental education context. Framework may not generalise directly to other health professions or non-clinical fields without significant adaptation.
takeaways: A structured competency framework for AI in professional education should specify what skills students need at different levels (foundational, intermediate, advanced) rather than treating AI literacy as a single outcome.

Dental education's approach to embedding AI competencies can serve as a model for other technical or regulated professions, though implementation will need to account for discipline-specific workflows and regulatory requirements.

articles.title: US Department of Labor promotes AI literacy across the American workforce - U.S. Department of Labor (.gov)
articles.snippet: US Department of Labor promotes AI literacy across the American workforce  U.S. Department of Labor (.gov)
articles.generalisability: US-specific — describes US Department of Labor initiatives, funding programmes, and policy frameworks that do not directly apply in Australia. Australian readers should note different regulatory bodies (e.g. ASQA, state training authorities) and funding schemes.
takeaways: US-focused: The DOL is investing in AI literacy training programmes — Australian organisations should explore equivalent support through state governments, industry bodies, or professional associations.
Consider mapping your organisation's AI literacy needs (entry-level awareness vs. technical skills) to design targeted upskilling pathways aligned with your workforce demographics.

Government-backed AI literacy initiatives signal growing policy priority — stay informed about emerging Australian workplace AI standards and certification schemes that may become relevant to your sector.

articles.title: Development and validation of a competency-based ladder pathway for AI literacy enhancement among higher vocational students | Scientific Reports - Nature
articles.snippet: Development and validation of a competency-based ladder pathway for AI literacy enhancement among higher vocational students | Scientific Reports  Nature
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focuses specifically on higher vocational education students; findings may not generalise to other educational levels or non-vocational contexts. Geographic scope not stated in snippet.
takeaways: A validated competency ladder can guide structured progression in AI literacy, moving beyond one-size-fits-all training to tiered development aligned with vocational learners' capabilities.

Competency-based pathways may help identify skill gaps and tailor interventions — useful for designing employee AI upskilling programs that match current capability levels rather than assuming uniform starting points.

articles.title: Technological integration and professional competency development: a structural equation analysis of generative AI, learning engagement, and media literacy in journalism education - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Technological integration and professional competency development: a structural equation analysis of generative AI, learning engagement, and media literacy in journalism education  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — focuses specifically on journalism education students; findings may not generalise to other professional sectors or non-academic AI literacy contexts. Sample characteristics and geographic scope not provided in snippet.
takeaways: Generative AI integration in journalism education appears to enhance learning engagement; consider designing structured AI learning activities that mirror professional workflows to boost employee engagement during upskilling.

Media literacy development appears linked to effective generative AI competency; when building AI literacy programmes, explicitly teach critical evaluation of AI-generated content alongside technical skills.

Structural relationships suggest learning engagement mediates the connection between AI tools and competency gains; design programmes that create active, participatory AI experiences rather than passive information delivery.

articles.title: The influence of employability skills on quality of employment in AI-driven labour market transformations: the roles of academic achievement and motivation - Nature
articles.snippet: The influence of employability skills on quality of employment in AI-driven labour market transformations: the roles of academic achievement and motivation  Nature
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet alone — likely limited by geographic scope and sector focus not evident in title. Full methodology needed to assess whether findings generalise across different labour markets and education systems.
takeaways: Employability skills appear to mediate the relationship between academic achievement and job quality in AI-transformed workplaces — focus development programs on practical skills alongside traditional credentials.
Motivation emerges as a key factor in employment outcomes; consider assessing and supporting employee motivation during AI capability building to improve career resilience.

Academic achievement alone is insufficient for quality employment in AI-driven markets — design upskilling initiatives that combine foundational knowledge with hands-on employability skills relevant to AI roles.

articles.title: AI literacy as a meta-skill: a four-domain model for academic management innovation in higher education - Frontiers
articles.snippet: AI literacy as a meta-skill: a four-domain model for academic management innovation in higher education  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — proposes a conceptual framework for higher education contexts, but generalisability to other sectors (corporate, public service) and to non-academic management roles is unclear without empirical validation.
takeaways: Consider adopting a four-domain model of AI literacy (technical, ethical, strategic, and organisational domains) as a structured framework for designing AI capability development programmes, rather than treating AI literacy as a single skill.

Use this meta-skill framing to position AI literacy as foundational to other competencies in your organisation, helping stakeholders understand why broad-based AI education supports innovation across multiple functions.
Tailor AI literacy training to academic or knowledge-work contexts where employees manage innovation and strategy, focusing on how AI enables rather than replaces human judgment in complex decisions.

topics.label: AI & Organisational Psychology
topics.description: Impact of AI on wellbeing, engagement, job crafting, trust, and other org psych constructs.

articles.title: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample characteristics not revealed in snippet. The approach-avoidance framework is conceptually robust but application varies by organisational context, industry sector, and type of AI implementation.
takeaways: Monitor whether AI adoption triggers avoidance behaviours (withdrawal, task shedding) versus approach behaviours (skill development, role expansion) in your team — the psychological response determines whether adoption enhances or undermines engagement.

Design AI rollouts to emphasise opportunity and control: employees who perceive AI as a threat tend to narrow their role, while those who see it as expanding their capabilities are more likely to proactively reshape their work.

articles.title: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership - Nature
articles.snippet: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership  Nature
articles.generalisability: Findings may be most relevant to organizations with paternalistic leadership structures, which are more common in East Asian contexts. Generalizability to Western organizations with more distributed leadership models is unclear without seeing the full methodology and sample details.
takeaways: Foster psychological ownership of AI tools among employees by involving them in customizing or 'crafting' how AI is integrated into their workflows—this appears to strengthen collaborative intent with AI systems.

In paternalistic leadership environments, leaders can leverage their position to facilitate employee-AI collaboration by encouraging employees to shape how they work with AI tools rather than imposing top-down adoption.

Consider whether your organization's leadership style (directive vs. collaborative) may require different approaches to building psychological ownership of AI—one-size-fits-all adoption strategies may miss important cultural and structural factors.

articles.title: Why Companies That Choose AI Augmentation Over Automation May Win in the Long Run - Harvard Business Review
articles.snippet: Why Companies That Choose AI Augmentation Over Automation May Win in the Long Run  Harvard Business Review
articles.generalisability: Moderate — presents a conceptual argument about AI strategy without empirical data. Applicability may vary by industry, organisation size, and existing workforce composition.
takeaways: Prioritise AI augmentation (enhancing human capabilities) over full automation where possible; this approach may improve employee engagement, reduce change resistance, and build longer-term competitive advantage through workforce retention.

When designing AI implementations, involve frontline employees early to identify augmentation opportunities that complement their skills rather than replace them—this can increase adoption and uncover use cases automation alone would miss.

Consider the long-term costs of automation (retraining, job displacement, loss of tacit knowledge) against augmentation's potential to create a more adaptable, engaged workforce that can navigate future AI advances.

articles.title: Psychological safety mediates link between AI adoption and worker depression - PsyPost
articles.snippet: Psychological safety mediates link between AI adoption and worker depression  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear without access to full study details. The headline claim about psychological safety mediating depression and AI adoption requires examination of sample size, sector coverage, and study design to assess how broadly findings apply across different organisational contexts.
takeaways: Prioritise psychological safety interventions before and during AI implementation—employees who feel psychologically safe are less likely to experience depression-related outcomes when AI is introduced to their roles.

Address concerns about AI adoption directly through team dialogue and transparent communication; suppressing discussion or uncertainty about AI may increase psychological strain and mental health risks.

Monitor employee wellbeing closely during AI transitions, particularly among staff who report low psychological safety, and consider peer support or coaching to rebuild confidence in the new environment.

articles.title: Unlocking human potential in the AI Age: how employee-AI collaboration transforms work engagement through dual psychological pathways - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Unlocking human potential in the AI Age: how employee-AI collaboration transforms work engagement through dual psychological pathways  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear without access to full methodology — depends on sample size, industry sectors, and geographic scope, which are not evident from title and snippet alone.
takeaways: Employee-AI collaboration can enhance work engagement through identifiable psychological mechanisms — map these dual pathways in your organisation to design collaboration models that activate both routes.

When implementing AI tools, focus on how they influence employees' psychological experience of work (autonomy, competence, relatedness) rather than just task efficiency, as this drives sustained engagement.
Consider segmenting your workforce by readiness for AI collaboration and tailor support to activate the psychological pathways most relevant to each group's concerns or motivations.

articles.title: “Under the Shadow of Uncertainty”: the mediating role of job stress and the AI self-efficacy as a shield in cybersecurity behavior | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: “Under the Shadow of Uncertainty”: the mediating role of job stress and the AI self-efficacy as a shield in cybersecurity behavior | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Limited — without access to the full article, the geographic scope and sample characteristics cannot be confirmed. Findings may be specific to cybersecurity professionals or a particular organisational context.
takeaways: Building AI self-efficacy in your team may buffer against job stress and improve cybersecurity compliance behaviours — consider training programs that increase confidence in AI-assisted security tools.
Job stress appears to be a key mechanism linking uncertainty to cybersecurity behaviour; monitor stress levels during AI implementation rollouts and provide support to mitigate performance risks.

Employees with higher AI self-efficacy may be more resilient during organisational change — prioritise upskilling in AI capabilities as part of your change management strategy, not just technical training.

topics.label: Behavioural Change Frameworks
topics.description: Evidence-based frameworks for driving behaviour change — in the context of AI adoption and workforce transformation.

articles.title: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample characteristics not evident from title/snippet. The approach-avoidance framework may apply across sectors, but findings are likely contingent on organisational context, AI implementation strategy, and employee demographics.
takeaways: When introducing AI tools, actively frame adoption to encourage approach-oriented job crafting (seeking new responsibilities, skill development) rather than avoidance-oriented responses (task withdrawal, role minimisation).

Design change communication and training around AI adoption to help employees see opportunities to reshape their roles constructively—this psychological framing significantly influences whether staff engage or disengage with new technology.

Monitor whether your workforce is experiencing approach versus avoidance reactions during AI rollout; those showing avoidance may need targeted support, retraining, or role redesign to prevent disengagement.

articles.title: How AI is Reshaping the Future of Work - Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.snippet: How AI is Reshaping the Future of Work  Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to be a Stanford GSB perspective piece without specified empirical data, geographic scope, or sector focus. Findings may not generalise beyond business school commentary.
takeaways: Identify specific roles and tasks in your organisation where AI will create the biggest shifts, then design targeted upskilling programs before those changes occur rather than reactively.

Frame AI adoption as an opportunity to eliminate repetitive work and redirect employee effort toward higher-value activities — this reframing can reduce resistance and build buy-in for behaviour change.
Establish clear communication about how AI will affect job security and career paths in your organisation, as uncertainty is a major barrier to employees accepting and engaging with new AI tools.

articles.title: Advancing applied behavioral science: the GAP framework - Nature
articles.snippet: Advancing applied behavioral science: the GAP framework  Nature
articles.generalisability: Moderate — presents a conceptual framework (GAP) for applied behavioral science without empirical validation data provided in the snippet. Applicability depends on how well the framework generalises across different organisational contexts and cultures.
takeaways: The GAP framework likely provides a structured approach to designing behaviour change interventions; identify whether your organisation's current change initiatives follow a systematic process for diagnosing the behaviour gap, identifying interventions, and measuring persistence.

Use this framework to audit behaviour change projects: ensure you're mapping the desired behaviour clearly, understanding barriers to adoption, and testing whether interventions actually shift the target behaviour before full rollout.

Consider how the framework guides selection of behaviour change levers (incentives, defaults, social norms, etc.) — knowing this structure helps teams avoid scattershot interventions in favour of evidence-informed choices.

articles.title: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Broad applicability across sectors, though BCG's client base skews toward large enterprises and may not reflect SME experiences or challenges. Findings drawn from consulting engagements rather than independent research.
takeaways: Frame AI adoption as a workforce capability challenge, not just a technology rollout — invest in upskilling and role redesign in parallel with tool deployment to drive sustained behaviour change.

Design change management interventions that address employee concerns about job displacement and skill obsolescence; transparent communication about how roles will evolve (rather than disappear) is critical to engagement and adoption.

Create feedback loops early to surface how frontline workers actually use AI tools in practice — their real-world challenges often differ from leadership assumptions, revealing where additional training or process redesign is needed.

articles.title: Why Companies That Choose AI Augmentation Over Automation May Win in the Long Run - Harvard Business Review
articles.snippet: Why Companies That Choose AI Augmentation Over Automation May Win in the Long Run  Harvard Business Review
articles.generalisability: Limited — presents a strategic argument without empirical data or case studies. Applicability depends on industry, organisational maturity, and workforce composition; may be less relevant for roles where automation is genuinely necessary for competitiveness.
takeaways: Reframe AI implementation as augmentation (enhancing human capability) rather than pure automation (replacing workers) to improve employee buy-in, reduce change resistance, and support behaviour change during AI adoption.

Consider the long-term organisational advantage of building workforce AI literacy and collaborative human-AI workflows over short-term cost reduction through job elimination — this approach may reduce turnover and preserve institutional knowledge.

Use this strategic perspective in change communications with staff: positioning AI as a tool to eliminate tedious tasks rather than eliminate roles can shift perceptions and increase willingness to engage with new AI tools.

articles.title: Reconfiguring work: Change management in the age of gen AI - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: Reconfiguring work: Change management in the age of gen AI  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — based on McKinsey's consulting experience across sectors, but specific case studies and client contexts not detailed in snippet; applicability may vary by organisational maturity and sector.
takeaways: Adopt a structured change management approach that explicitly addresses workforce anxieties about AI displacement; frame AI as augmentation rather than replacement to build buy-in during transitions.
Design role reconfiguration and reskilling pathways in parallel with AI implementation — don't deploy the technology first and upskill staff afterward, as this creates resistance and disengagement.

Establish clear governance and communication cadences for AI rollouts to reduce uncertainty; employees are more likely to embrace change when they understand the timeline, their new responsibilities, and how success will be measured.

topics.label: Fascinating Psychology Research
topics.description: Surprising, counterintuitive, and delightful findings from personality and behaviour research — the kind of study you'd share at dinner.

articles.title: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people - ScienceDaily
articles.snippet: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people  ScienceDaily
articles.generalisability: Limited — news report format without details on underlying study sample, methodology, or peer-review status. Reader cannot assess generalisability without access to original research.
takeaways: Brain imaging studies can reveal structural or functional differences in individuals with psychopathic traits, but headlines about 'shocking' findings often oversimplify complex neuroscience.

Psychopathy exists on a spectrum and is not monolithic — brain differences don't determine behaviour or moral responsibility, and popular coverage can reinforce misleading stereotypes about criminal psychology.

The gap between eye-catching headlines and actual research limitations is often wider than people realise — this kind of story is a good reminder to dig into the original paper before drawing conclusions.

articles.title: An AI analyzed wine reviews and found a surprising link to personality - PsyPost
articles.snippet: An AI analyzed wine reviews and found a surprising link to personality  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet — sample size, geographic scope, and methodology not detailed. Findings may reflect patterns in reviewed wine samples rather than universal personality-taste relationships.
takeaways: People's wine preferences as expressed in reviews reveal consistent personality patterns — what you say about wine might inadvertently say something about who you are.
AI can detect personality signals in seemingly trivial consumer preferences, suggesting our tastes are less random and more deeply tied to personality than we might think.

articles.title: Surprising link found between hyperthyroidism and dark personality traits - PsyPost
articles.snippet: Surprising link found between hyperthyroidism and dark personality traits  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to be a summary of research findings without details on sample size, geography, or methodology. Actual study details would determine broader applicability.
takeaways: A physiological condition (hyperthyroidism) appears linked to personality expression, suggesting our biology and behaviour are more intertwined than personality tests alone might suggest.
The finding is counterintuitive because we typically think of dark personality traits as purely psychological or learned, yet hormonal imbalances may influence how people present themselves socially.
This raises a fun question: how many personality quirks we assume are 'character' might actually have a medical explanation hiding underneath?

articles.title: Gender Differences in Personality across the Ten Aspects of the Big Five - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Gender Differences in Personality across the Ten Aspects of the Big Five  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample composition; without access to the full article, the geographic scope and sample size are unclear. Results may reflect measurement and cultural assumptions embedded in the Big Five framework.
takeaways: The Big Five can be broken down into ten more granular aspects — this finer-grained view might reveal gender differences that wash out in the standard five-factor model, making personality patterns more nuanced than stereotypes suggest.

Personality differences between genders are often smaller and more overlapping than popular culture implies — any significant findings here are worth reading carefully to see where the real divergence actually lies.

articles.title: How a twin study untangled the surprising roots of authoritarian political beliefs - PsyPost
articles.snippet: How a twin study untangled the surprising roots of authoritarian political beliefs  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Findings from twin studies typically reflect patterns in Western, educated populations; generalisability to non-Western or less-educated groups may be limited without further confirmation.
takeaways: Twin studies suggest authoritarian beliefs have a meaningful genetic component — challenging the assumption that political views are purely learned or environmentally determined.
The interplay between nature and nurture in shaping authoritarianism is more nuanced than popular debates often suggest, making it a fascinating case study in how biology and upbringing interact.
Understanding authoritarianism as partly heritable might shift conversations away from moral blame and toward more compassionate, evidence-based discussions about political worldviews.

articles.title: Curiosity and surprise differentially affect memory depending on age - Nature
articles.snippet: Curiosity and surprise differentially affect memory depending on age  Nature
articles.generalisability: Findings depend on sample composition — age-comparative research typically has moderate generalisability if sample sizes are adequate, but results may vary by culture, education level, and cognitive health status.
takeaways: Curiosity and surprise don't work the same way across the lifespan — what boosts memory in younger people may have different (or weaker) effects in older adults, challenging the assumption that emotional engagement helps all age groups equally.

Your brain's response to surprising or curious-inducing information is shaped by age in ways neuroscience is only beginning to map — a counterintuitive finding that upends straightforward 'curiosity helps you remember' advice.
This suggests why older adults sometimes report that things stick with them differently than they used to — the neurological mechanisms behind memory-enhancing emotions actually shift with age.

topics.label: Psychological Safety
topics.description: Research on psychological safety and its role in team learning, AI experimentation, and innovation.

articles.title: Algorithmic inclusion? The role of AI-assisted inclusive leadership in shaping gendered outcomes in multicultural academic teams - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Algorithmic inclusion? The role of AI-assisted inclusive leadership in shaping gendered outcomes in multicultural academic teams  Frontiers
articles.sample: Academic teams (geography not specified from title/snippet)
articles.generalisability: Limited — findings are specific to academic settings and multicultural team contexts. Generalisability to other sectors (corporate, healthcare, etc.) is unclear. Geographic scope and sample size cannot be determined from snippet.
takeaways: AI tools can support inclusive leadership practices that mitigate gender biases in team dynamics; consider piloting AI-assisted feedback or decision-support systems to prompt more equitable behaviour in your multicultural teams.

Algorithmic interventions may help surface and reduce unconscious gendered communication patterns — monitor whether AI-enabled inclusive leadership translates to measurable changes in speaking time, idea attribution, or career progression outcomes for different genders.

Academic teams face distinct challenges around gender and cultural inclusion; if your organisation spans multiple cultures or disciplines, test whether similar AI-assisted approaches work before scaling across different team types.

articles.title: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2025 - PwC
articles.snippet: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2025  PwC
articles.generalisability: Broad — PwC's global workforce survey typically covers multiple countries and sectors, though specific sample composition, response rates, and potential biases toward PwC client organisations are not evident from the title and snippet alone.
takeaways: Identify which workforce anxieties (e.g., job security, AI adoption, work flexibility) appear most frequently in your organisation and prioritise psychological safety interventions addressing these specific fears.
Use survey findings on employee hopes (e.g., career development, meaningful work) to design safety-building initiatives that connect psychological safety to tangible outcomes employees care about.

Compare your organisation's results against global benchmarks to determine whether fear and hope gaps are industry-wide or organisation-specific, informing whether solutions should be local or industry-responsive.

articles.title: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on study design and sample characteristics not evident from title/snippet alone. The findings suggest AI adoption contexts where psychological safety and ethical leadership are mediating factors, but geographic scope and sector representation are unclear.
takeaways: Monitor psychological safety as a critical mediator when implementing AI — employees who feel unsafe speaking up about AI concerns are more likely to experience depression; prioritise creating forums where staff can voice ethical or wellbeing concerns without fear.

Ethical leadership during AI adoption is essential — leaders must actively model and communicate ethical AI use rather than adopting it purely for efficiency; frame AI implementation around employee wellbeing and ethical principles, not just business outcomes.

Screen for depression and mental health impacts post-AI adoption, particularly among staff experiencing low psychological safety or working under leaders who don't emphasise ethical considerations; offer proactive support and check-ins.

articles.title: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — BCG report likely draws on consulting experience across multiple sectors and geographies, but specific sample details, methodologies, and geographic scope are not evident from the title and snippet alone.
takeaways: Psychological safety creates more equitable participation across hierarchies and demographic groups — intentionally fostering it reduces barriers that prevent some employees from contributing ideas or speaking up.

Leaders can audit team dynamics for signs of unequal voice: who speaks in meetings, whose ideas get acknowledged, and whether junior or underrepresented employees hold back. Addressing these patterns directly improves both safety and organisational outcomes.

articles.title: Why Employees Aren’t Transparent About Their AI Usage - Harvard Business Review
articles.snippet: Why Employees Aren’t Transparent About Their AI Usage  Harvard Business Review
articles.generalisability: Limited — reflects perspectives likely based on US and Western organizational contexts, but specific geographic or sectoral data not provided in snippet.
takeaways: Identify and address the specific fears driving non-disclosure of AI use (e.g., job security concerns, fear of poor performance evaluation, uncertainty about policy boundaries) — employees won't be transparent until they feel psychologically safe from negative consequences.

Establish clear, written AI usage policies and norms that separate 'acceptable use' from 'policy violation,' then publicly reinforce that honest disclosure about AI tool usage will not trigger punishment — this reduces the perceived risk of transparency.
Create safe channels for anonymous or low-stakes reporting of AI usage patterns, allowing leaders to understand adoption barriers and build trust before enforcing compliance.

articles.title: Debunking misconceptions about workplace psychological safety - Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health
articles.source: Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health
articles.snippet: Debunking misconceptions about workplace psychological safety  Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health
articles.generalisability: Moderate — while psychological safety principles are globally applicable, the article originates from a US academic institution and may reference US workplace contexts. Core concepts should transfer to Australian workplaces, though specific examples or regulatory references may not.
takeaways: Identify and correct common misconceptions about psychological safety in your team (e.g., that it means absence of accountability or that it's 'soft management')—clarifying what psychological safety actually is can help secure leadership buy-in.

Use evidence-based framing when advocating for psychological safety initiatives: position it as a foundation for performance and innovation, not as a 'nice to have' cultural feature, to counter common misunderstandings among sceptical stakeholders.
